Level 100 core: Business Communication (BUS101); Introduction to Accounting (BUS103); Economics (BUS104); Commercial Law (BUS107); Skills for Numerical Analysis (BUS109)
Level 200 core: Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MAN202)
Level 300: no compulsory core subjects — students select electives across accounting, marketing, management, hospitality and IT streams, including Internship 1 (BUS307) and Internship 2 (BUS308)
Structure: 24 subjects across 9 trimesters, full-time, 3 years; five intakes per year
Delivery: Adelaide, Brisbane, Melbourne, Perth, Sydney
admission_requirements: Completion of Year 12 (Australian Senior Secondary Certificate) or equivalent, ATAR approx. 65-75 (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: Bachelor of Business (Accounting)
description:
This is the accounting-major version of KBS's Bachelor of Business, and the accounting content only really kicks in once the shared foundation year is out of the way. The first five subjects (business communication, intro accounting, economics, commercial law, numerical analysis) are identical to every other Bachelor of Business student at KBS, and the single Level 200 core (governance, ethics and sustainability) is also shared. What makes this a genuine accounting degree rather than a business degree with an accounting flavour is the block of electives students are steered toward at Level 200 and 300: financial accounting, management accounting, taxation law, auditing, and corporate law units that map onto what CPA Australia and CA ANZ expect to see for graduates seeking a pathway into the CPA Program or CA ANZ's professional entry route.

Students who complete this major and want to go further don't have to leave KBS to do it: the school's Master of Accounting picks up where this degree leaves off and carries its own accreditation from CPA Australia, CA ANZ and ACCA, so a student can plan a five-year run from school leaver to professionally accredited accountant without changing institutions. That continuity matters more here than in some of the school's other majors, since accounting is one of the few fields where the professional body's unit-mapping requirements genuinely shape what gets taught rather than the university choosing freely.

Like the rest of the Bachelor of Business suite, the degree runs on trimesters (nine trimesters, 24 subjects, three years full-time) with five intakes a year, and the two Level 300 internship subjects give accounting-track students a chance to sit inside a firm before graduating rather than only after.
curriculum:
Level 100 core (shared foundation): Business Communication (BUS101); Introduction to Accounting (BUS103); Economics (BUS104); Commercial Law (BUS107); Skills for Numerical Analysis (BUS109)
Level 200 core: Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MAN202)
Accounting major electives (Level 200-300): Financial Accounting; Management Accounting; Taxation Law; Auditing and Assurance; Business and Corporations Law; Financial Reporting
Level 300 options: Internship 1 (BUS307); Internship 2 (BUS308)
Structure: 24 subjects across 9 trimesters, full-time, 3 years
Delivery: Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney (accounting major availability varies by campus — confirm current intake)
admission_requirements: Completion of Year 12 (Australian Senior Secondary Certificate) or equivalent, ATAR approx. 65-75 (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: Bachelor of Business (Hospitality and Tourism Management)
description:
This is the outlier in the KBS Bachelor of Business family: instead of accounting, marketing or management electives layered onto the generalist core, students stack hospitality and tourism operations subjects, covering areas like hospitality service management, tourism destination planning, event management and hospitality law. It sits under subject area codes distinct from the rest of the business suite for a reason: tourism and hospitality in Australia is a genuinely separate industry with its own regulatory and seasonal quirks (visa-dependent international student labour, tourism board relationships, hotel and events sector cyclicality) that a generic business degree doesn't really touch.

The shared foundation is identical to every other Bachelor of Business student at KBS: communication, accounting, economics, commercial law and numerical analysis in Level 100, governance/ethics/sustainability at Level 200. Where this major earns its name is in the Level 200-300 stream, which brings in operations-focused units aimed at hotel, resort, tourism board, airline and events employers rather than the corporate management track. The two internship subjects at Level 300 do a lot of work here, since hospitality and tourism hiring in Australia still runs heavily on demonstrated on-the-job experience, and a KBS internship placement in this major is more likely to land in a hotel, resort or tourism operator than a corporate office.

Graduates commonly move into hotel and resort management, event coordination, tourism marketing or destination management roles, and the degree's international student intake (KBS runs large cohorts from source markets like India, Nepal and China) means classroom discussion of hospitality service standards tends to draw on a genuinely global range of hospitality norms rather than an Australia-only frame.
curriculum:
Level 100 core (shared foundation): Business Communication (BUS101); Introduction to Accounting (BUS103); Economics (BUS104); Commercial Law (BUS107); Skills for Numerical Analysis (BUS109)
Level 200 core: Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MAN202)
Hospitality and Tourism Management major electives: Hospitality Service Management; Tourism Destination Planning; Event Management; Hospitality Law and Risk; Rooms Division and Resort Operations; Tourism Marketing
Level 300 options: Internship 1 (BUS307); Internship 2 (BUS308) — commonly placed with hotel, resort or tourism operators
Structure: 24 subjects across 9 trimesters, full-time, 3 years
Delivery: check current campus availability; historically concentrated at Sydney and Melbourne
admission_requirements: Completion of Year 12 (Australian Senior Secondary Certificate) or equivalent, ATAR approx. 65-75 (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: Bachelor of Business (Management)
description:
The management major is the most conventional read of KBS's Bachelor of Business: it takes the shared foundation (business communication, accounting, economics, commercial law, numerical analysis, then governance/ethics/sustainability) and layers on the Level 300 subjects the school specifically flags as its advanced management core: dynamic strategy, entrepreneurship, creativity and innovation, management in global business, and managing change. That's a more deliberately generalist manager-track than the accounting or marketing majors, aimed at students who want to move into supervisory and management roles across any industry rather than a functional specialism.

One practical caveat: KBS notes that its Management and Marketing programs aren't currently available at the Brisbane and Perth campuses, so this major is realistically an Adelaide, Melbourne or Sydney option at present. The Level 300 subjects reappear as MBA elective options too (dynamic strategy and entrepreneurship in particular), so a student who does this major as an undergraduate and later returns for an MBA at KBS will recognise some of the same subject titles at a more advanced level, which is either a nice continuity or a reason to look elsewhere for genuinely new content, depending on how you view it.

As with the rest of the suite, it's 24 subjects across nine trimesters, full-time three years, with the two Level 300 internship subjects available to build workplace experience before graduating, useful for a major where a management job title tends to require some demonstrated track record even at graduate level.
curriculum:
Level 100 core (shared foundation): Business Communication (BUS101); Introduction to Accounting (BUS103); Economics (BUS104); Commercial Law (BUS107); Skills for Numerical Analysis (BUS109)
Level 200 core: Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MAN202)
Level 300 management core: Dynamic Strategy; Entrepreneurship; Creativity and Innovation; Management in Global Business; Managing Change
Level 300 options: Internship 1 (BUS307); Internship 2 (BUS308)
Structure: 24 subjects across 9 trimesters, full-time, 3 years
Delivery: Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney (not currently offered at Brisbane or Perth campuses)
admission_requirements: Completion of Year 12 (Australian Senior Secondary Certificate) or equivalent, ATAR approx. 65-75 (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: Bachelor of Business (Marketing)
description:
Marketing at KBS sits on top of the same generalist foundation as every Bachelor of Business student (communication, accounting, economics, commercial law, numerical analysis in the first year, one ethics and governance subject in the second), and then diverges through a run of Level 200 and 300 electives built around consumer behaviour, digital and social media marketing, brand strategy and marketing analytics. The degree isn't marketed with a heavy digital-first pitch the way some newer marketing degrees are; it reads more as a traditional marketing major that has folded digital channels and analytics in as electives rather than rebuilding the whole degree around them, which suits students who want a broad marketing grounding rather than a narrowly digital one.

One practical note for anyone comparing campuses: KBS states plainly that its Marketing (and Management) programs aren't currently offered at the Brisbane and Perth campuses, so students set on this major need to check availability at Adelaide, Melbourne or Sydney before enrolling. The two Level 300 internship subjects are open to marketing-track students and are one of the more direct ways to turn the degree into agency or in-house marketing experience before graduation, given how heavily entry-level marketing hiring in Australia still leans on demonstrated placement or agency exposure.

As with the rest of the Bachelor of Business family, it's a 24-subject, nine-trimester degree with five intake points a year, which in practice means a student starting in a November intake finishes roughly three years later without waiting on the standard February/July university calendar.
curriculum:
Level 100 core (shared foundation): Business Communication (BUS101); Introduction to Accounting (BUS103); Economics (BUS104); Commercial Law (BUS107); Skills for Numerical Analysis (BUS109)
Level 200 core: Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MAN202)
Marketing major electives (Level 200-300): Consumer Behaviour; Marketing Communications; Digital and Social Media Marketing; Brand Management; Marketing Analytics; Services Marketing
Level 300 options: Internship 1 (BUS307); Internship 2 (BUS308)
Structure: 24 subjects across 9 trimesters, full-time, 3 years
Delivery: Adelaide, Melbourne, Sydney (not currently offered at Brisbane or Perth campuses)
admission_requirements: Completion of Year 12 (Australian Senior Secondary Certificate) or equivalent, ATAR approx. 65-75 (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: Graduate Diploma of Business Administration
description:
The Graduate Diploma of Business Administration is best understood as roughly the front half of the KBS MBA, packaged as a standalone exit point. Students who want postgraduate business credentials but aren't ready to commit to the full 12-subject MBA, whether for cost, time, or visa-related reasons, take a subset of the same core leadership, governance and financial literacy units plus a smaller elective load, and finish with a qualification that's also directly stackable: KBS structures the Grad Diploma so that credit carries across into the MBA if a student later decides to continue.

In practice this credential does two jobs for two different kinds of students. It's an exit award for people partway through the MBA who need to leave study early with something to show for it, and it's also a deliberate entry point for students whose undergraduate degree or work background doesn't quite clear the bar for direct MBA admission, giving them a shorter, lower-stakes program to demonstrate postgraduate-level capability before stepping up. Either way, it shares the trimester structure and multi-campus footprint of the rest of the KBS postgraduate suite.

Because it's shorter than the MBA, there's less room for elective specialisation, so the degree leans on the shared core (leadership and people management, governance and ethics, and financial/economic literacy for managers) rather than offering the eight-track specialisation menu the full MBA carries.
curriculum:
Core subjects: People, Culture and Contemporary Leadership (MBA401); Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MBA402); Financial and Economic Interpretation and Communication (MBA403)
Electives (selected from the MBA elective pool): typically drawn from Consumer Behaviour and Marketing Psychology, Dynamic Strategy, International Business, Project Management
Structure: 8 subjects, shorter than the full 12-subject MBA; credit pathway into the MBA for students who continue
Delivery: Adelaide, Brisbane, Gold Coast, Melbourne, Perth, Sydney, or online
admission_requirements: Relevant bachelor's degree (or equivalent); some programs consider work experience in lieu (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: Master of Accounting
description:
KBS built the Master of Accounting with triple accreditation in mind: CPA Australia, Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand, and ACCA all recognise it, which for an international student cohort matters more than it might for domestic-only accounting programs, since it gives graduates a credential that's portable if they end up practising outside Australia. At 16 subjects across six trimesters (two years full-time), it's a heavier load than the school's other master's degrees, reflecting how much technical ground a professionally accredited accounting qualification has to cover: financial and management accounting, financial reporting, auditing and assurance, corporations law, taxation law, and a dedicated accounting information systems unit.

What's distinctive is how far the elective list leans into analytics rather than traditional accounting electives: students choosing from strategic management accounting, data visualisation, data acquisition and management, AI and machine learning, and business analytics project management, alongside a more conventional internship option. That reflects a broader shift in how accounting firms hire: the analytics-minded electives are clearly there to produce graduates who can sit inside a Big Four or mid-tier firm's advisory or analytics practice, not just its audit or tax compliance teams.

The capstone, Accounting and Governance, closes the degree by pulling the technical subjects together into governance and reporting judgement calls rather than pure technical computation. It's the kind of synthesis a CPA or CA ANZ pathway expects graduates to demonstrate before they're considered ready for the professional program's practical experience requirements.
curriculum:
Core subjects (13): Financial Accounting; Management Accounting; Advanced Financial Accounting; Financial Reporting; Auditing and Assurance; Information Systems in Accounting; Business and Corporations Law; Taxation Law; Economics; Finance; Analytics in Accounting and Finance; Quantitative Methods; Capstone: Accounting and Governance
Electives (choose 3): Strategic Management Accounting; Introduction to Business Analytics; Data Visualisation and Communication; Data Acquisition and Management; Data Security and Ethics; Data-driven Forecasting; Marketing and Social Media Analytics; Business Analytics Project Management; Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning; Innovation and Creativity in Business Analytics; Internship
Accreditation: CPA Australia, Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (CA ANZ), ACCA
Structure: 16 subjects across 6 trimesters, full-time, 2 years
Delivery: Adelaide, Brisbane, Gold Coast, Melbourne, Sydney, Perth
admission_requirements: Relevant bachelor's degree (or equivalent); some programs consider work experience in lieu (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: Master of Business Administration
description:
Kaplan Business School runs its MBA on a trimester clock rather than the semester rhythm most Australian universities use, so a full-time student can finish 12 subjects in two years across six trimesters spread over campuses in Adelaide, Brisbane, Gold Coast, Melbourne, Perth and Sydney, plus an online cohort for anyone juggling the degree around a job. The six core subjects lean toward the interpersonal and interpretive side of management: leadership, governance and ethics, financial and economic literacy for non-finance managers, consumer psychology, and a cross-cultural intelligence unit that reflects how much of the cohort tends to be international postgraduates working alongside local managers already in industry.

What separates it from a generic MBA is the elective architecture. Rather than a single fixed specialisation, students pick six electives (or condense that to three plus a three-subject specialisation block) from a list that spans dynamic strategy, entrepreneurship, international business, digital marketing, project management, healthcare and tourism management, and an internship placement. KBS picked up a PIEoneer award in 2020 for its approach to flexible content delivery, and the specialisation model is really an extension of that: eight named specialisation tracks, from Data-driven Leadership to Women in Leadership, let two people graduate with the same base MBA and quite different transcripts.

The degree closes with a capstone strategy subject that asks students to work a live business problem end to end, drawing on the core units rather than treating strategy as an abstract elective. For students who already hold significant industry experience, Recognition of Prior Learning can shorten the path, which matters for a program whose average student profile skews toward people returning to study mid-career rather than straight out of an undergraduate degree.
curriculum:
Core subjects: People, Culture and Contemporary Leadership (MBA401); Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MBA402); Financial and Economic Interpretation and Communication (MBA403); Consumer Behaviour and Marketing Psychology (MBA404); Emotional Intelligence, Cultural Intelligence and Diversity (MBA502); MBA Capstone: Strategy (MBA600)
Electives (choose six, or three plus a three-subject specialisation): Dynamic Strategy, Entrepreneurship, International Business, Digital Marketing, Project Management, Tourism and Hospitality Management, Healthcare Management, Analytics electives, Internship
Optional specialisation tracks (replace three electives): Data-driven Leadership, Project Management, Health Services Management, Tourism and Hospitality Leadership, Digital Management, Entrepreneurship, International Leadership, Women in Leadership
Structure: 12 subjects across 6 trimesters, full-time, 2 years standard pace; part-time and accelerated options available
Delivery: Adelaide, Brisbane, Gold Coast, Melbourne, Perth, Sydney campuses, or fully online
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree (any discipline) typically required; relevant work experience preferred (approximate, typical bar, not program-page-verified)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall (typical bar for postgrad at private AU providers, approximate)

name: Master of Business Analytics (Information Technology)
description:
The Information Technology stream of KBS's Master of Business Analytics builds on the same core analytics subjects as the standard degree (data acquisition, visualisation, security and ethics, forecasting, AI and machine learning, quantitative methods) but points the elective and specialisation choices toward IT infrastructure and systems concerns rather than purely commercial analytics applications. At five trimesters (one year eight months) full-time, it's noticeably shorter than KBS's Master of Accounting, reflecting the more compact, technically-focused nature of the analytics field compared with a professionally accredited accounting qualification.

The degree closes with an Analytics Capstone built around an industry research project, which in the IT-focused variant tends to mean students working through a genuine data or systems problem sourced from an organisation rather than a synthetic classroom case, and it's positioned by the school as substantial preparation for further postgraduate study as much as direct employment, since KBS notes it carries credit into related postgraduate IT and analytics courses elsewhere.

Graduates from this stream typically move into business analyst, data/reporting analyst or business intelligence roles, sitting at the intersection of the commercial decision-making side of analytics (forecasting, marketing analytics, project management) and the more technical AI/machine learning and data security content. It's a combination that suits students who want to work with data teams without retraining as software engineers or data scientists from scratch.
curriculum:
Core subjects (9): Introduction to Business Analytics; Data Visualisation and Communication; Data Acquisition and Management; Data Security and Ethics; Data-driven Forecasting; Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning; Analytics in Accounting and Finance; Quantitative Methods; Analytics Capstone: Industry Research Project
Electives (choose 3, IT-focused): Artificial Intelligence Programming in Business Analytics; Business Analytics Project Management; Marketing and Social Media Analytics; Innovation and Creativity in Business Analytics; Internship
Structure: 12 subjects across 5 trimesters, full-time, 1 year 8 months
Delivery: Adelaide, Brisbane, Gold Coast, Melbourne, Perth, Sydney
admission_requirements: Relevant bachelor's degree (or equivalent); some programs consider work experience in lieu (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: MBA (Health Services Management)
description:
This is the health services specialisation running inside KBS's standard MBA chassis: same six core subjects on leadership, governance, financial literacy, consumer behaviour and cultural intelligence, capped off with the same strategy capstone, but three of the elective slots are swapped for a dedicated health services management block. That's a meaningful distinction from a standalone Master of Health Administration: students here graduate with an MBA, not a health-specific credential, which suits people aiming for general management roles inside hospitals, aged care providers or health insurers rather than clinical or health-policy careers specifically.

The specialisation content covers managing healthcare teams, service delivery models and the operational and workforce pressures particular to the sector: rostering clinical staff, navigating funding models tied to Medicare and private health insurance, and the compliance load that comes with operating in a heavily regulated industry. Given how much of Australia's health workforce is trained overseas and re-credentialed locally, and how many KBS postgraduate students are themselves international, the cohort composition for this specialisation tends to include a real mix of people already working clinically who want a move into management, alongside career changers from unrelated industries.

It runs on the same trimester calendar as the base MBA (12 subjects, six trimesters, two years full-time), with the option to compress or extend the pace, and is offered across the same national campus network plus online delivery.
curriculum:
Core subjects (shared with base MBA): People, Culture and Contemporary Leadership (MBA401); Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MBA402); Financial and Economic Interpretation and Communication (MBA403); Consumer Behaviour and Marketing Psychology (MBA404); Emotional Intelligence, Cultural Intelligence and Diversity (MBA502); MBA Capstone: Strategy (MBA600)
Health Services Management specialisation electives (three subjects): Healthcare Systems and Policy; Managing Health Services Teams; Health Service Operations and Funding
Remaining electives: chosen from the general MBA elective list (Dynamic Strategy, International Business, Digital Marketing, Project Management, Internship, etc.)
Structure: 12 subjects across 6 trimesters, full-time, 2 years standard pace
Delivery: Adelaide, Brisbane, Gold Coast, Melbourne, Perth, Sydney, or online
admission_requirements: Relevant bachelor's degree (or equivalent); some programs consider work experience in lieu (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: MBA (Project Management)
description:
Project Management is one of the eight specialisation tracks layered onto KBS's standard MBA structure, and it's aimed squarely at students who want PM methodology and credentials attached to a general management degree rather than a narrower Master of Project Management. The six core MBA subjects (leadership, governance, financial literacy, consumer behaviour, cultural intelligence, and the strategy capstone) stay the same; what changes is three of the elective slots, replaced with subjects covering the full project lifecycle: initiation and scoping, risk analysis, team leadership under project constraints, and evaluating project outcomes against original business cases.

KBS pitches the specialisation as "industry-informed," and in practice that shows up in the electives sitting alongside genuinely commercial content rather than an academic treatment of PMBOK theory alone. Students in this track often pair the project subjects with electives in digital marketing or business analytics to build toward specific industries (construction, IT delivery, health infrastructure) rather than treating project management as a discipline in isolation. That flexibility is really the point of doing this as an MBA specialisation instead of a dedicated postgraduate PM degree: graduates come out with the broader people-management and strategy grounding of an MBA, with project delivery skills as the differentiator on top.

Same trimester structure as the base MBA: 12 subjects, six trimesters, two years full-time, available across the national KBS campus network and online, with Recognition of Prior Learning available for students who've already managed projects professionally and can demonstrate it against specific subjects.
curriculum:
Core subjects (shared with base MBA): People, Culture and Contemporary Leadership (MBA401); Governance, Ethics and Sustainability (MBA402); Financial and Economic Interpretation and Communication (MBA403); Consumer Behaviour and Marketing Psychology (MBA404); Emotional Intelligence, Cultural Intelligence and Diversity (MBA502); MBA Capstone: Strategy (MBA600)
Project Management specialisation electives (three subjects): Project Initiation and Scoping; Project Risk Analysis; Leading Project Teams
Remaining electives: chosen from the general MBA elective list (Dynamic Strategy, Digital Marketing, Business Analytics, International Business, Internship)
Structure: 12 subjects across 6 trimesters, full-time, 2 years standard pace
Delivery: Adelaide, Brisbane, Gold Coast, Melbourne, Perth, Sydney, or online
admission_requirements: Relevant bachelor's degree (or equivalent); some programs consider work experience in lieu (approximate, typical bar)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall, no band below 6.0 (approximate, typical bar)

name: Bachelor of Arts
description:
La Trobe's Bachelor of Arts covers an unusually wide humanities and social sciences spread for a Melbourne university, with archaeology standing out as a genuine area of departmental strength. La Trobe has run archaeology programs and fieldwork opportunities (including Australian and international excavation sites) for decades, well before most other Victorian universities built comparable programs. Criminology, politics, sociology, history, creative writing, journalism and a suite of language majors round out the available options.

Students build the degree around a major (occasionally two) plus a broad elective spread, and the course sits within a university that also runs La Trobe's Australian Institute for Public Policy and Innovation, giving politics and public policy students some connection to genuine policy research happening on campus rather than a purely theoretical curriculum.
curriculum:
Major (typically 8 subjects) chosen from Archaeology, Criminology, History, Politics and Policy Studies, Sociology, Creative Writing, Journalism, Languages (including options such as Indonesian, Italian, Spanish), and others
Second major or minor from a related discipline
Core Arts foundation subjects in critical thinking and research methods
Work-integrated learning or fieldwork component (notably in Archaeology)
Elective subjects to complete the degree
Honours pathway available in most majors for students proceeding to postgraduate research
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Business
description:
La Trobe Business School's Bachelor of Business sits within a AACSB-accredited faculty, which puts it in a smaller group of Australian business schools holding that particular international accreditation. Majors span the standard commerce disciplines: accounting, finance, marketing, management, human resource management, and the degree is taught across multiple La Trobe campuses (Bundoora in Melbourne, plus regional delivery at Bendigo, Albury-Wodonga, Shepparton and Mildura), which matters for the practical experience, since placement opportunities and industry partners differ noticeably depending on which campus a student is based at.

Work-integrated learning runs through the degree via La Trobe's industry-based learning program, connecting students with real organisations rather than leaving professional experience to a single capstone unit. The accounting major in particular is accredited by CPA Australia and Chartered Accountants ANZ, giving graduates a direct line into the CA/CPA pathway.
curriculum:
Business core: Accounting for Managers, Economics for Business, Marketing Principles, Business Law, Management, Business Statistics
Major (choose one or two) from Accounting, Finance, Marketing, Management, Human Resource Management
Industry-based learning/work-integrated learning subject
Elective subjects and a second major or minor
Capstone: Business Strategy or Consultancy Project
AACSB-accredited business school; Accounting major accredited by CPA Australia and CA ANZ
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Commerce - Bachelor of Psychological Science
description:
This combined degree pairs La Trobe Business School's commerce core with the university's APAC-accredited psychological science stream, aimed at students who want a genuine double credential rather than a psychology minor tacked onto a business degree. It runs longer than either component alone, and the pairing shows up in career outcomes that are less obvious than a straight psych or straight commerce path: organisational psychology, HR analytics, and consumer behaviour research roles draw specifically on graduates who can do both the statistics-heavy psychology research methods sequence and a genuine accounting or marketing major.

Because the psychological science component still needs to satisfy APAC's Level 1 competency requirements, students don't get to water down the psych side to make room for commerce. Both halves are taught to the same standard as the standalone degrees, which is why the combined degree takes longer to complete than either on its own.
curriculum:
Commerce component: Business core (Accounting, Economics, Marketing, Management) plus a commerce major (e.g. Marketing, HR Management, Finance)
Psychological Science component: full APAC Level 1 sequence — Introduction to Psychology, Biological and Cognitive Psychology, Developmental and Social Psychology, Research Methods and Statistics
Integrated capstone or research project drawing on both disciplines
Elective units to complete the combined degree's extended credit point total
APAC-accredited psychology component; pathway to Honours for registration-track students
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Engineering (Honours)
description:
La Trobe's engineering school is considerably younger than its Business or Science faculties. Its first engineering cohorts only began in the mid-2010s, and the course was built from the ground up around a project-based learning model rather than a traditional lecture-and-tutorial structure inherited from an older program. Students work through substantial team-based engineering projects in most years of the degree rather than treating design projects as a single capstone experience bolted onto a lecture-heavy course.

Majors are offered across the conventional engineering disciplines, and the course is run from the Bundoora campus with strong emphasis on industry partnerships for placements, reflecting the practical, employer-facing approach La Trobe has taken to differentiate a newer engineering school from long-established Group of Eight competitors in Melbourne.
curriculum:
Year 1: Engineering Fundamentals, Engineering Mathematics, Engineering Mechanics, first team-based engineering project
Years 2–3: major-specific technical subjects (Civil, Electrical, Mechanical, or Mechatronic engineering), continued project-based subjects each year
Industry placement/work-integrated learning component
Year 4: capstone engineering design project, undertaken in industry-partnered teams
Accredited pathway to Engineers Australia professional recognition
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion with strong mathematics; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Information Technology
description:
The undergraduate Bachelor of Information Technology follows the same specialisation logic as La Trobe's postgraduate IT courses, with majors in areas like cybersecurity, software development, networking and data-oriented computing, delivered mainly from the Bundoora campus with a Sydney campus option for students in NSW. Core first-year subjects cover programming fundamentals, systems and networks, and database design before the major-specific content takes over from second year.

La Trobe has pushed cybersecurity hard as a growth area across both its undergraduate and postgraduate IT offerings, reflecting genuine industry demand in Melbourne's tech and finance sectors, and the degree carries ACS accreditation that gives graduates a recognised route into Australian Computer Society membership. A capstone industry project or placement unit in the final year is standard rather than optional, tying the technical major to an applied deliverable before graduation.
curriculum:
Year 1 core: Introduction to Programming, Computer Systems and Networks, Database Design, ICT Professional Practice
Major (from Year 2) chosen from Cybersecurity, Software Development, Networking, or Data-oriented computing streams
Elective units and a minor from a complementary discipline
Capstone: industry project or work placement in final year
ACS-accredited
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Nursing
description:
La Trobe's standard Bachelor of Nursing places students into clinical environments from first year, drawing on the university's long-standing partnerships with major Victorian health providers, including Austin Health, the Royal Women's Hospital, and Bendigo Health, rather than waiting until later years to start placements. The 800 clinical placement hours run across acute care, chronic illness management, mental health, rehabilitation, community and emergency settings, and the course also carries a specific First Nations Health subject and an Indigenous health component woven into the broader curriculum, not treated as a standalone add-on.

Students are required to purchase a branded scrub top for placements, a small but telling detail of how seriously the clinical placement component is treated administratively. Since July 2025, eligible students on mandatory placements can access the Australian Government's Commonwealth Prac Payment, which matters in practice given how placement blocks affect a nursing student's ability to hold down paid work during those weeks.
curriculum:
Year 1: Foundations of Nursing Practice, Anatomy and Physiology, Biosciences for Nursing, first clinical placement block
Year 2: Acute Care Nursing, Chronic Illness Management, Mental Healthcare in Nursing, Primary Healthcare, Research in Nursing, continued placements
Year 3: Rehabilitation and Community Nursing, Emergency Care, First Nations Health, capstone Transition to Professional Practice placement
800 hours of clinical placement across partner health services including Austin Health, Royal Women's Hospital, and Bendigo Health
Eligible for AHPRA registration as a Registered Nurse on completion; Commonwealth Prac Payment eligibility for placement periods from July 2025
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 7.0 (no band below 7.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Psychological Science
description:
La Trobe's Bachelor of Psychological Science is the university's APAC-accredited foundation pathway into professional psychology, and it benefits from a research environment that's genuinely notable in one specific area: the Olga Tennison Autism Research Centre (OTARC), based at La Trobe, is one of the country's leading autism research groups, and its work feeds directly into some of the developmental and clinical psychology content taught in the degree.

The course covers the standard APAC Level 1 competencies, including biological bases of behaviour, cognition, developmental and social psychology, and research methods and statistics, and sets students up for La Trobe's own fourth-year Honours program, the compulsory next step for anyone pursuing provisional psychologist registration or further clinical postgraduate training. Students who want a psychology qualification without the accreditation pathway typically choose the psychology major within the Bachelor of Arts or Science instead; this degree is specifically for those aiming at registration.
curriculum:
Core subjects: Introduction to Psychology, Biological Psychology, Cognitive Psychology, Developmental Psychology, Social Psychology, Research Methods and Statistics (sequence across years 1–3), Abnormal Psychology, Psychological Assessment
Minor or elective sequence outside psychology
Research project/capstone subject in final year
APAC-accredited, meeting Level 1 competencies for provisional psychologist registration pathway
Progression to Bachelor of Psychological Science (Honours), the required fourth year for registration
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Data Science
description:
The Master of Data Science mirrors the IT masters' two-year, 240-credit-point structure, with a 1.5-year accelerated pathway for anyone holding a cognate degree in data science, AI or IT. Core subjects front-load the mathematical and programming groundwork (data exploration and analysis, database fundamentals, introductory programming, mathematics and probability/statistics for data science) before students branch into a genuinely varied elective list covering bioinformatics, sport analytics, big data and cloud computing, and business applications.

The sport analytics option is a distinctive inclusion tied to La Trobe's sport and exercise science strength (the university runs a well-regarded sport science program out of Bundoora), giving data science students a specialisation that isn't just a rebadged AI or business analytics track. Delivery is multi-modal, blending online and on-campus study, which suits the working-professional segment of the cohort who are retraining into data careers mid-career.
curriculum:
Core subjects: Data Exploration and Analysis, Database Fundamentals, Introduction to Programming, Mathematics for Data Science, Probability and Statistics for Data Science, Professional Practices and Entrepreneurship in IT
Elective/specialisation subjects in Artificial Intelligence, Bioinformatics, Sport Analytics, Big Data and Cloud Computing, or Business Applications and Data Modelling
Capstone data science project
240 credit points over 2 years standard; 180 credit points/1.5 years for cognate-entry applicants
Multi-modal (online and on-campus) delivery
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree with quantitative background
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Information Technology
description:
La Trobe's Master of IT runs on a 240 credit point, two-year structure by default, but drops to 180 points and 18 months for anyone entering with a cognate Australian bachelor's degree in computer science, IT or information systems, a meaningful shortcut that a lot of applicants coming from a non-technical undergraduate background don't get. Foundational subjects in database logic, programming, network engineering and cybersecurity run early, with entrepreneurship and project management folded in as transferable skills rather than treated as an afterthought elective.

Where the degree earns its ACS accreditation is in the specialisation list, which reaches further than a typical Australian IT masters: artificial intelligence, cloud analytics, cybersecurity, Internet of Things, networking, software engineering, and, less commonly offered, quantum information technology. That last one reflects La Trobe's investment in quantum computing research at its Bundoora campus rather than being a token addition to a course list.
curriculum:
Foundational subjects: Database Logic and Data Structures, Programming, Network Engineering, Cybersecurity Fundamentals
Professional skills subjects: Professional Practice, Project Management, Entrepreneurship in IT
Specialisation (choose one): Artificial Intelligence, Cloud Analytics, Cybersecurity, Internet of Things, Networking, Quantum Information Technology, or Software Engineering
Elective subjects to complete the credit point total
Capstone project or industry-based subject in final year
240 credit points over 2 years standard; 180 credit points/18 months for cognate-entry applicants
ACS-accredited
admission_requirements: Australian bachelor's degree (or equivalent), 240cp/2yr pathway (any discipline), or 180cp/1.5yr pathway (cognate: computer science, IT, or information systems).
english_requirements: IELTS Academic 6.5 overall, no band below 6.0.

name: Master of Nursing Science
description:
The Master of Nursing Science is La Trobe's postgraduate pathway for registered nurses seeking a specialist clinical qualification rather than a management-focused credential. Students typically move into specialisations like perioperative nursing, primary health care, or mental health nursing, drawing on La Trobe's clinical partnerships including its affiliated clinical school arrangement with Austin Health in Melbourne's north-east.

Because candidates already hold RN registration, the degree assumes a working clinical base and builds advanced practice knowledge and research skills on top of it, rather than repeating undergraduate nursing content. Part-time study while continuing to work clinically is the norm rather than the exception, and the course structure accommodates that with a mix of online coursework and clinically-oriented practicum or advanced placement components tied to the chosen specialisation.
curriculum:
Core subjects: Advanced Nursing Practice, Research Methods in Health Sciences, Evidence-Based Practice, Health Care Ethics and Policy
Specialisation stream (choose one): Perioperative Nursing, Primary Health Care, or Mental Health Nursing
Advanced clinical/practicum component tied to chosen specialisation
Elective subjects to complete the degree
Research project or minor thesis in final stage
Delivered via clinical partner network including La Trobe's affiliation with Austin Health
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree in a health-related discipline
english_requirements: IELTS 7.0 (no band below 7.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Actuarial Studies
description:
Actuarial studies at Macquarie is built directly against the Actuaries Institute's exemption framework rather than as a general quantitative degree that happens to touch on actuarial topics. Strong performance in the relevant units can earn exemptions from the Institute's Foundation Program subjects (CM1, CM2, CS1, CS2, CB1, CB2) and the Actuary Program's ACC and DSP subjects, which shortens the professional qualification path students face after graduation, a meaningful head start given how long the full actuarial credentialing process typically takes on top of any degree.

The department has also been recognised as a Center of Actuarial Excellence by the US-based Society of Actuaries, a status held by a limited number of programs globally, which gives the degree standing for students who might end up working in US, UK or Asian insurance and superannuation markets rather than only the Australian one. Macquarie Business School's AACSB accreditation applies here too, on top of the actuarial-specific recognition.

Students completing the degree as part of a double degree, paired with Applied Finance, Science, or Information Technology, and achieving credit or higher in the relevant units become eligible for exemptions from both the Foundation and Actuary Program subjects, which is one reason the actuarial-plus-finance or actuarial-plus-IT combination shows up so often among Macquarie's actuarial cohort rather than students taking the single degree alone.
curriculum:
Core sequence: mathematics for actuarial studies, probability and statistics, life contingencies, financial mathematics, actuarial modelling, economics for actuaries, actuarial statistics
Advanced units: risk theory, general insurance, financial risk management, investment and asset modelling
Accreditation: recognised by the Actuaries Institute, with exemption eligibility for Foundation Program subjects CM1, CM2, CS1, CS2, CB1, CB2 and Actuary Program subjects ACC, DSP
Recognition: Department of Actuarial Studies and Business Analytics holds Center of Actuarial Excellence status from the Society of Actuaries (US)
Structure: 3 years full-time; frequently combined as a double degree with Applied Finance, Science or Information Technology
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion with strong mathematics; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Arts
description:
Macquarie's Bachelor of Arts is genuinely broad rather than a single-discipline degree with a generic label. Majors span history, philosophy, international studies, media, English, politics, ancient history, linguistics and a long list of languages, and students commonly combine two majors rather than committing to one, similar to how the Commerce degree is structured. The Faculty of Arts is one of the university's larger faculties and its ancient history and Egyptology programs in particular have a reputation that draws students from well outside Sydney specifically for that specialisation, a genuine point of distinction few other Australian BA programs can match.

Like every Macquarie undergraduate degree, the BA carries a compulsory PACE unit, so arts students end up with a documented placement or community-engagement project on their transcript rather than the degree being purely classroom-based, which matters for a cohort often steered (fairly or not) toward assumptions about limited direct career pathways. Students planning postgraduate study in a specific humanities discipline, or aiming at teaching, law, journalism or public service career tracks, typically use the major and elective combination to build toward those follow-on qualifications rather than treating the BA as a terminal generalist credential.

The degree also functions as the entry point for language study leading toward Macquarie's translation and interpreting postgraduate programs, since a number of the languages taught at undergraduate level (Chinese, French, Japanese, Korean, Spanish) map directly onto the postgraduate NAATI-accredited pathway.
curriculum:
Structure: choose one or two majors from a wide list including History, Philosophy, International Studies, Media, Communication and Cultural Studies, English, Politics and International Relations, Ancient History, Linguistics, and languages (Chinese, French, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, and others)
Foundational units: discipline-specific first-year sequences depending on chosen major(s)
PACE unit: compulsory work-integrated or community engagement placement
Electives: free choice across faculties
Structure: 3 years full-time, 24 units total; can be combined with Laws, Commerce, Education or other degrees
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Commerce
description:
The Bachelor of Commerce at Macquarie starts everyone on the same broad foundation year across accounting, economics, business law and quantitative methods before students pick one or two majors from a list running through accounting, finance, marketing, management, business analytics, actuarial studies, economics and international business, among others. Combining two majors rather than one is common here, and the degree is explicitly built to make that pairing work rather than treating a second major as an awkward add-on, which is one reason it draws students who aren't sure yet whether they want to end up in finance, marketing or something more analytical.

What distinguishes it structurally from a lot of other commerce degrees is the compulsory PACE unit, Professional and Community Engagement, a Macquarie-wide requirement that places students with a real organisation to work on an actual problem for course credit rather than a simulated case study. For commerce students that typically lands as a capstone-adjacent internship experience, so most graduates leave with at least one documented piece of workplace experience already on the resume before they've applied for a graduate role.

Macquarie Business School carries AACSB accreditation, held by a minority of business schools worldwide, which matters for students weighing this degree against a less internationally recognised commerce program when they're thinking about working or studying further afield after graduation.
curriculum:
Foundation units: financial and management accounting basics, microeconomics and macroeconomics, business law, quantitative methods and statistics for business, business communication
Majors (choose one or two): Accounting, Finance, Marketing, Management, Business Analytics, Actuarial Studies, Economics, International Business, Human Resource Management, and others
PACE unit: compulsory work-integrated internship or community engagement placement, typically embedded as a capstone experience
Electives: free choice across the Business School and other faculties
Structure: 3 years full-time, 24 units total
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Engineering (Honours)
description:
Macquarie's engineering honours degree runs on five accredited specialisations (Mechanical, Mechatronic, Software, Civil, and Electrical and Electronic Engineering), all recognised by Engineers Australia, with the Software Engineering stream carrying additional accreditation from the Australian Computer Society. That Engineers Australia stamp is what makes the qualification recognised across North America, and much of Asia and Europe through mutual recognition agreements, which matters for a cohort that includes a substantial number of international students planning careers outside Australia.

What sets the degree apart in practice is Macquarie's PACE program, which the university treats as a genuine point of differentiation rather than a token add-on: engineering students get placed with real firms to work on live technical problems, and Macquarie Park's cluster of engineering, tech and infrastructure employers sitting a short walk from campus makes those placements more accessible here than at universities without an equivalent employment precinct next door. The honours component isn't a bolt-on fourth year either. It's integrated through the degree, culminating in a substantial final-year design or research project specific to the chosen specialisation.

Students can also combine the engineering degree with Commerce or Science as a double degree, which is common enough at Macquarie that dedicated combined-degree pages exist for those pairings, aimed at students who want engineering credentials alongside a business or science major rather than choosing between them.
curriculum:
Common engineering core (early years): engineering mathematics, mechanics, materials, engineering design, programming for engineers, professional engineering practice
Specialisation (choose one, accredited by Engineers Australia): Mechanical Engineering; Mechatronic Engineering; Software Engineering (also accredited by the Australian Computer Society); Civil Engineering; Electrical and Electronic Engineering
Work-integrated learning: PACE placement units with industry partners
Final year: capstone engineering design/research project specific to specialisation
Structure: 4 years full-time honours degree; combinable as a double degree with Commerce or Science
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion with strong mathematics/physics; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Psychology
description:
This is Macquarie's APAC-accredited undergraduate psychology sequence, and the accreditation detail matters more than it might for other degrees: without a program recognised by the Australian Psychology Accreditation Council, graduates can't progress toward provisional or general registration as a psychologist in Australia at all. The three-year degree covers the discipline broadly, from cognitive and biological psychology through developmental, social and abnormal psychology, before students who want to continue toward registration move into the honours year.

That honours year isn't automatic. Admission requires a weighted average grade of 70 across all psychology units and 75 across 300-level psychology units specifically, with a minimum of 72 credit points completed, and it only starts in first semester, running two semesters as an intensive research year built around an individually supervised thesis. For students who don't clear that bar or don't want to pursue registration, the base three-year degree still stands on its own as a psychology qualification, just not one that leads directly into professional practice.

Given how competitive honours entry is nationally in psychology (the accreditation bottleneck limits places at every Australian university, not just Macquarie), students aiming for registration are generally advised to treat the 300-level grade threshold as a first-year planning consideration rather than something to worry about only in third year.
curriculum:
Core sequence: introduction to psychology, biological psychology, cognitive psychology, developmental psychology, social psychology, abnormal psychology, research methods and statistics I-III
300-level advanced units: personality, health psychology, forensic psychology, neuropsychology (options vary by year)
Honours year (separate admission, weighted average 70 overall / 75 at 300-level required): advanced research methods, supervised empirical thesis, specialist seminars
Accreditation: Australian Psychology Accreditation Council (APAC) — required pathway toward provisional psychologist registration
Structure: 3-year bachelor's degree; honours year (2 semesters, February entry only) as a separate accredited add-on
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; ATAR as per current guide
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Applied Finance
description:
Applied Finance at Macquarie runs through a five-unit core covering corporate finance, financial instruments, financial risk management, investments and a professional practice unit, then branches into one of four specialisations: Funds Management, Risk Management, Corporate Finance, or Instruments and Valuation, drawing on a pool of more than 30 elective units. That elective depth is unusually large for a finance master's and reflects the program's history as much as anything: it grew out of what's now the Macquarie Applied Finance Centre, a specialist unit within the Business School built specifically around finance practitioner education rather than finance being one specialisation inside a general MBA.

The degree is recognised by the CFA Institute, which for a program this finance-specific matters more directly than it would for a general MBA, since CFA recognition speaks to how closely the curriculum tracks the CFA's own body of knowledge in valuation, portfolio management and financial analysis. Less common electives in sustainable finance and resources, infrastructure and energy finance sit alongside the four core specialisations, which reflects Sydney's position as a hub for both green finance and natural resources project financing, giving students in those tracks a genuinely local industry pipeline rather than an imported curriculum.

Given Macquarie's own history and its association with Macquarie Group (one of the world's largest specialist investment banks, no formal ownership link but a strong professional and reputational connection through name and alumni networks), the degree draws heavily on finance industry practitioners as guest lecturers and adjunct staff, which shapes it toward practitioner-oriented, market-relevant content over purely academic finance theory.
curriculum:
Core units (5): Corporate Finance; Financial Instruments; Financial Risk Management; Investments; Professional Practice
Specialisation (choose one, from 30+ elective units): Funds Management; Risk Management; Corporate Finance; Instruments and Valuation
Additional elective areas: Sustainable Finance; Resources, Infrastructure and Energy Finance
Recognition: CFA Institute recognised program
Structure: full-time or part-time; typically 1.5-2 years full-time equivalent
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree or equivalent
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Business Administration
description:
Macquarie's MBA sits inside a business school carrying AACSB accreditation, a marker held by roughly the top 6 percent of business schools globally, and the degree draws heavily on the school's applied finance and actuarial research strength, meaning the finance and analytics electives here tend to have more genuine quantitative depth than the equivalent electives at a generalist MBA program. Sydney's Macquarie Park location also puts the cohort within easy reach of the corporate campuses of Optus, Canon, Cochlear and a string of other multinationals headquartered in the same business park, and networking events and guest lectures lean on those neighbours more than a CBD-based MBA program typically can.

The program follows the standard MBA architecture of a core management and leadership sequence, covering strategy, finance, marketing and organisational behaviour, layered with electives that let students angle the degree toward general management, finance or a more analytics-heavy track depending on career direction. As with Macquarie's undergraduate degrees, PACE-style industry engagement is woven into the postgraduate experience through consulting projects and industry-based capstone work rather than confined to a single elective.

Students coming from a non-business undergraduate background (engineering, science, health) are a substantial share of the intake, which shapes classroom discussion toward translating technical or clinical expertise into management responsibility rather than assuming everyone arrives with a commerce background already.
curriculum:
Core units: managerial economics, financial management, strategic management, marketing management, organisational behaviour and leadership, business analytics for decision making
Electives: chosen to build a general management, finance, or analytics-focused profile — options include corporate finance, digital marketing, supply chain management, entrepreneurship
Capstone: applied strategy or consulting project, often with an industry partner
Accreditation: Macquarie Business School holds AACSB accreditation
Structure: full-time or part-time options; typically 1.5-2 years full-time equivalent
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree plus relevant work experience
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Data Science
description:
The Master of Data Science covers the standard core of the field, statistical and machine learning methods, data management, programming and data visualisation, but the structural detail worth knowing is Macquarie's zone system: a core zone of compulsory units everyone completes, and a capstone unit specifically flagged in the handbook (units carrying a C designation) that requires students to apply the degree's technical content to a substantial project rather than close out with another taught unit. That capstone is where the degree earns its applied reputation, typically built around a dataset and problem sourced from industry or a research partner rather than a synthetic classroom exercise.

As a two-year full-time degree it runs longer than some competitor data science master's programs, which reflects Macquarie positioning it partly as an entry pathway for students without a quantitative undergraduate background (commerce, life sciences, humanities graduates retraining into data roles) rather than purely as an advanced technical top-up for computer science graduates. Students entering with a stronger quantitative or programming background can typically move through the foundational content faster and spend proportionally more time on the machine learning and advanced statistical modelling units toward the end of the degree.

Macquarie Business School's Department of Actuarial Studies and Business Analytics has a hand in aspects of the analytics curriculum here, which shows up in a stronger-than-average statistical modelling and risk-analytics flavour compared with data science programs housed purely in a computer science faculty.
curriculum:
Core zone: programming for data science, statistical methods, data management and databases, data visualisation, machine learning fundamentals, applied research methods
Advanced units: predictive modelling, big data technologies, natural language processing or deep learning (options vary by intake)
Capstone unit (C-coded): applied data science project, typically with an industry or research partner
Electives: drawn from business analytics, computing, or statistics depending on background and interest
Structure: full-time, typically 2 years; shorter with recognised prior study in a quantitative discipline
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree with quantitative background
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Information Technology
description:
Macquarie compresses what would be a three-year undergraduate IT degree into the first year of this master's, then spends the second year on advanced, specialised content, which is how the university frames it for the large share of students entering from an unrelated bachelor's degree, commerce or the humanities, say, without prior computing study. That two-speed structure only really works because of the zone system: a foundation zone for students who need to pick up programming and systems fundamentals from scratch, a core zone shared by everyone, and a flexible zone where the specialisation and electives sit.

Three specialisations are on offer: Artificial Intelligence, Cyber Security and Information Systems. The AI stream goes into machine learning, natural language processing and the ethical and legal questions that come with deploying AI systems in production rather than treating those as an afterthought unit. Cyber Security covers digital forensics, ethical hacking and information security operations, aimed at students heading toward SOC analyst, penetration testing or security engineering roles rather than pure compliance work. Information Systems sits closer to enterprise IT strategy and systems management for students aiming at business-facing technology roles.

Students finishing the degree can choose between a supervised research project and an industry internship as their final applied component, a genuinely different choice depending on whether the plan is a PhD application or a fast track into an employer's graduate program. Given Macquarie's location next to the Macquarie Park tech and business precinct (home to a dense cluster of multinational tech and engineering firms), the internship route in particular tends to draw on placements that wouldn't be as accessible from a campus further from Sydney's northern tech corridor.
curriculum:
Year 1 (accelerated foundation, for students without an IT background): programming fundamentals, data structures and algorithms, systems analysis and design, database systems, networking fundamentals
Year 2 core: advanced software engineering, cloud computing, applied research methods in IT
Specialisation (choose one): Artificial Intelligence (machine learning, natural language understanding, AI ethics and law); Cyber Security (information security, digital forensics, ethical hacking, data privacy); Information Systems (enterprise systems, IT strategy and governance)
Flexible zone: electives within or outside the IT discipline
Final component: supervised research project or industry internship
Structure: full-time, typically 2 years (1.5 years with recognised prior study)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree in a relevant or any discipline (typical Australian postgrad IT/CS entry bar used as approximate default, not program-specific verified).
english_requirements: IELTS Academic 6.5 overall, no band below 6.0 (typical postgrad bar used as approximate default, not program-verified).

name: Master of Research in Cyber, Policing, Intelligence, Counter Terrorism, Security Studies and Criminology
description:
This is a research degree, not a coursework master's, and that distinction matters more here than in most program listings: Macquarie's Master of Research (MRes) is explicitly built as a training pathway toward a PhD or Master of Philosophy rather than a standalone professional qualification, and this particular award lets students specialise their research within the Department of Security Studies and Criminology across cyber security, policing, intelligence, counter terrorism, security studies or criminology. Anyone weighing this against Macquarie's separate coursework Master of Cyber-Security, Policing, Intelligence and Counter Terrorism should understand these are genuinely different degrees serving different purposes, one trains researchers, the other trains practitioners.

The structure runs in two parts across two years full-time: a Graduate Diploma year (Part A) of intensive coursework building research skills specific to the discipline, followed by a second year (Part B) spent producing a roughly 20,000-word thesis on a self-defined research problem within the security, policing or criminology space. Admission to progress from MRes to a doctorate depends directly on the final MRes mark: a mark of 65-74% typically supports progression to an MPhil, while 75% and above supports progression to a full PhD, so the second-year thesis grade functions as a genuine gatekeeping mechanism rather than a formality.

Given Macquarie's Department of Security Studies and Criminology sits within a policy-facing research environment with strong Canberra and law-enforcement links, students often use the MRes thesis to build a body of original research on an Australian security or policing problem that then carries directly into a funded PhD project, rather than starting a doctorate from a blank slate.
curriculum:
Part A (Year 1, Graduate Diploma level): research methods and design, discipline-specific advanced seminars in security studies, criminology, policing or counter terrorism, literature review and research proposal development
Part B (Year 2): supervised original research culminating in an approximately 20,000-word thesis
Specialisation areas: Cyber Security, Policing, Intelligence, Counter Terrorism, Security Studies, Criminology (student selects a research focus within the department)
Progression outcomes: final mark 65-74% supports progression to Master of Philosophy (MPhil); 75%+ supports progression to PhD
Structure: 2 years full-time (or 4 years part-time)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree with honours or equivalent research background
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Translation and Interpreting Studies
description:
Macquarie's translation and interpreting program is approved by NAATI, Australia's national accrediting body for translators and interpreters, at professional level, which is the credential that actually lets graduates work as certified translators or interpreters in Australia rather than simply having studied the field academically. Students choose a language pair with English from Chinese (Mandarin), French, Japanese, Korean or Spanish, and the coursework runs alongside a separate, more specialised Master of Conference Interpreting for students aiming specifically at simultaneous interpreting careers rather than the broader translation and interpreting scope covered here.

Because NAATI accreditation is assessed against specific competency standards rather than general coursework completion, the degree is built around practical translation and interpreting exercises, legal and medical interpreting scenarios, ethics and professional conduct, alongside the linguistic theory underpinning translation practice, rather than treating professional accreditation as a separate add-on qualification students pursue after finishing an academic degree.

Sydney's demographic mix, with large first-generation communities across the five language pairs on offer, means placement and practicum opportunities for students in this program are unusually concrete: court interpreting, community health interpreting and settlement services all draw on graduates of programs exactly like this one, which is a different career pipeline from the conference and diplomatic interpreting track that the separate Master of Conference Interpreting targets.
curriculum:
Core units: translation theory and practice, interpreting theory and practice, professional ethics and conduct for translators/interpreters, consecutive and simultaneous interpreting techniques
Applied practicum units: legal interpreting, medical/health interpreting, community and liaison interpreting, specialised translation (legal, technical, business texts)
Language pairs available: Chinese (Mandarin), French, Japanese, Korean, Spanish (paired with English)
Accreditation: NAATI professional-level approval, subject to satisfying program requirements
Structure: typically 1.5 years full-time (18 months)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree or equivalent, proficiency in a second language
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Business
description:
MIT structures its Bachelor of Business so students spend the first year on a broad common core before locking in a major (Contemporary Management, Business Analytics, Marketing and Digital Communications, or Accounting), which gives students who arrive unsure of specialisation a genuine runway to figure it out rather than committing on day one. The Accounting major specifically feeds into professional body accreditation pathways (CPA Australia, CAANZ), which matters for international students planning to stay in Australia and pursue accounting as a migration occupation.

As with MIT's other degrees, the pitch here isn't research prestige. It's practical, industry-connected teaching delivered in smaller classes than a large public university, with a flipped-classroom format and the InSPIRE academic support scheme built specifically around a cohort that skews heavily international. The Business Analytics major overlaps meaningfully with MIT's dedicated Bachelor of Data Analytics, so prospective students choosing between the two need to look closely at how much of each degree is data/technical versus general business content.

MIT runs three intakes a year and offers the degree from both its Melbourne and Sydney campuses, which is a point of flexibility not available at most Australian universities tied to a single February/July semester cycle.
curriculum:
Year 1 (common core): Principles of Management, Marketing Fundamentals, Accounting for Business, Business Economics, Business Law, Business Statistics
Majors (choose one, Years 2-3): Contemporary Management, Business Analytics, Marketing and Digital Communications, Accounting
Capstone: industry-based project or internship in final year
Total: 3 years full-time, 360 credit points, on campus (Melbourne or Sydney), 3 intakes per year
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; foundation/diploma pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Data Analytics
description:
MIT's Bachelor of Data Analytics is built around what the university calls a flipped classroom model: students work through material before class so contact time can go toward applied, hands-on problem-solving rather than lecture delivery, combined with the InSPIRE academic support program aimed at helping students, many of them international, adjust to Australian tertiary assessment expectations. The degree covers the full data analytics lifecycle from data collection through to AI and machine learning applications, rather than treating machine learning as an advanced elective bolted onto a traditional stats degree.

The standout structural feature is the final year, where students complete two separate industry-based capstone projects rather than one, each running through the full systems development lifecycle (specification, analysis, design, development, implementation, testing, troubleshooting) with real industry supervisors involved alongside academic staff. That's a heavier applied-project load than a lot of comparable data analytics undergraduate degrees carry, and it's consistent with MIT's institutional identity as a work-integrated-learning-first provider rather than a research-intensive university.

As a private provider without the research profile of a larger public university, MIT's practical positioning here works well for students who want a direct, applied path into data analyst roles without a heavy theoretical statistics or computer science load.
curriculum:
Core units: Data Science Fundamentals, Programming for Data Analytics, Database Systems, Statistical Methods, Machine Learning Fundamentals, Data Visualisation, Big Data Technologies, Ethics and Governance in Data
Capstone: two industry-based projects in final year, each covering the full analytics/systems development lifecycle
Total: 3 years full-time, on campus (Melbourne or Sydney)
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; foundation/diploma pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Engineering Technology (Telecommunications)
description:
This is the undergraduate, engineering-technologist-level counterpart to MIT's Master of Engineering (Telecommunications): a slightly more applied, hands-on qualification pitched at students who want to work directly with telecommunications infrastructure rather than pursue the more theory-heavy professional engineer accreditation track. The degree runs 24 units totalling 360 credit points, with each standard unit worth 15 credit points, and covers planning, design, implementation and maintenance of telecommunication systems using current hardware and software rather than legacy equipment.

One core unit specifically worth noting is applied mobile and satellite communication systems, covering antennas, microwaves, GPS, and spectrum analysis. That's specialised content that doesn't show up in a generic electrical or IT degree and reflects genuine subject-matter depth in a fairly narrow technical niche. A twelve-week full-time (or 24-week part-time) industry placement is mandatory rather than optional, consistent with MIT's institution-wide emphasis on work-integrated learning, and gives graduates direct workplace telecommunications experience before they finish the degree.

The program is TEQSA-accredited (Australia's higher education regulator), and electives in IT, security, and information systems let students round out the core telecommunications content with adjacent technical skills that broaden employability beyond a single carrier-network-engineer career track.
curriculum:
Core units (24 total, 15 credit points each): Telecommunications Fundamentals, Network Design and Infrastructure, Wireless and Broadband Networks, Applied Mobile and Satellite Communication Systems, Signal Processing, Telecommunications Regulation and Standards, plus IT/security/information systems electives
Work-integrated learning: mandatory 12-week full-time (or 24-week part-time) industry placement
Total: 360 credit points, standard full-time load 60 credit points per trimester (approx. 3 years full-time), TEQSA-accredited, on campus
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion with mathematics; foundation/diploma pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent
